newsitem.title: USA: U.S. factory orders fell 1.6 percent in March.
newsitem.headline: U.S. factory orders fell 1.6 percent in March.

text.p: Orders received by U.S. factories in March took their biggest tumble since last summer, reflecting broad-based declines in demand for manufactured goods, the Commerce Department said on Tuesday.

The 1.6 percent drop in March orders to a seasonally adjusted $319.21 billion followed a smaller-than-previously estimated 0.4 percent rise in February orders. Wall Street economists had forecast a 1.5 percent decline in March orders.
Despite the March decline, factory orders so far this year are still running 5.7 percent ahead of their 1996 pace.
The March order decline, the biggest since a 2.1 percent drop last August and the first reduction this year, comes amid expectations of a slowdown in manufacturing.
The industrial sector chugged along at a busy 84.1 percent of its capacity in March and in April its workers put in for record-high overtime.
But economists expect that factory output would begin to slack off later in the year in part because of a build-up of inventories that must be worked off.

Manufacturers' inventories rose 0.2 percent to $442.73 billion in March, the eighth rise in the last nine months, while order backlogs registered their first drop since last August, declining 0.4 percent to $520.12 billion, the department said.

Shipments of manufactured goods, which reflect more immediate demand than orders, slipped 0.1 percent to $321.15 billion in March after a 0.9 percent rise in February but are still running 6.7 percent ahead of last year's pace, the department said.

Last week, the department estimated that durable goods orders, long-lasting items that account for about half of total factory business, fell 3 percent in March. It revised that in the factory orders report to show a slightly less severe 2.6 percent drop.
Orders for non-durable goods slid 0.3 percent in March after a 0.4 percent setback in February.
Among the largest declines was a drop in orders for transportation equipment, which fell 4.6 percent in March after plunging 7.2 percent in February.
Shipments of motor vehicles and parts fell 1.8 percent in March after a 1.9 percent drop in February. In the automobile industry, shipments correspond to orders.
Excluding transportation, factory orders fell 1.2 percent in March after rising in February by 1.5 percent.
Orders for non-defence capital goods, a measure of business' expansion plans, declined by 4 percent in March, but were still running barely ahead of last year's pace.
Defence contractors' orders, which are subject to wide monthly swings, dropped by 13.7 percent after an 11.1 percent decline in February.
Excluding defence industries, factory orders were down 1.4 percent in March after rising 0.6 percent in February.
Orders for industrial machinery fell 1 percent after a 2 percent rise in February, while bookings for electronic and electrical equipment fell 4.9 percent in March after a 7.8 percent gain.
One of the few major industrial categories that saw an increase in orders was primary metals, where bookings rose 0.3 percent after a 0.5 percent drop in February.
